title: Drinking water reports and inclusionary zoning update
subtitle: Receivable write-offs, water quality plan re-endorsement, and housing questions on Bill 23 and affordability tools.
overview: The committee recommended that two sets of uncollectable accounts be written off: $8,781 in miscellaneous receivables and $80,371 in utility receivables. Both were carried {{vote:m1}} {{vote:m2}}.

On drinking water, the committee recommended re-endorsing the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard Operational Plan, as required at the start of a new term of Council {{vote:m3}}. It also received the 2022 management review summary and the 2022 Summary Drinking Water Report for information {{vote:m4}} {{vote:m5}}. The report is to be shared with the Township of Woolwich and the City of Waterloo. Staff said an audit recommended recertification and that there are no concerns with the system.

Most of the meeting was spent on an information report on inclusionary zoning for affordable housing, which requires some new developments to include affordable units. No motion was needed. Staff said provincial changes under Bill 23 are expected to limit the program and are not yet in force. Staff expect to bring recommendations to Council around the end of the second quarter. Councillors also asked about transition rules, rental supply, family-sized units and affordability monitoring.

decisions.detail: The committee recommended writing off $8,781 in uncollectable miscellaneous receivable accounts against the Allowance for Doubtful Receivables {{vote:m1}}.
The committee recommended writing off $80,371 in uncollectable utility accounts against the allowance for doubtful utility receivables {{vote:m2}}.
The committee recommended re-endorsing the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard Operational Plan under the Safe Drinking Water Act, 2002 and Regulation 188/07 {{vote:m3}}.
The committee received the 2022 Drinking Water Quality Management Standard Management Review Summary for information {{vote:m4}}.
The committee received the 2022 Summary Drinking Water Report for information and directed that a copy go to the Township of Woolwich and the City of Waterloo {{vote:m5}}.

debate: Staff said Bill 23 and proposed regulations would cap the share of units that can be required as affordable, limit affordability to 25 years, and set the lowest price or rent at 80% of market. These are not yet in force. Inclusionary zoning units are already exempt from development charges, parkland dedication and community benefits charges.

Councillors raised the slow rollout and the transition rules. Staff said complete applications filed before the policy takes effect are sheltered under the Planning Act. Staff added that the delay comes from waiting on provincial approval of the region's protected major transit station areas.

One councillor said the policy would not solve the housing shortage and that effort should go to seeking funding from other levels of government. Others said inclusionary zoning is one of the few tools a lower-tier municipality has and should not be dropped. Staff described ongoing advocacy to the federal and provincial governments.

Councillors asked about family-sized units, build costs and monitoring. Staff said three-bedroom units are cheaper to deliver in stacked townhouses than in high-rises, and a missing middle study is expected in April. Staff said affordability agreements can be registered on title but monitoring will be an administrative burden.
A councillor asked about discolouring of water near the Strange Street treatment plant. Staff said there had been very few such reports since the upgrades, fewer than before.
